questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: Which estimate is not realistic?
questions.stemText: Which estimate is not realistic? A The power of a computer laptop is 50 W. B The kinetic energy of a car is 100 MJ. C The mass of a sheet of A4 paper is 5 g. D The heating element of an iron has a temperature of 500 K.

options.label: A
options.text: The power of a computer laptop is 50 W.

options.label: B
options.text: The kinetic energy of a car is 100 MJ.

options.label: C
options.text: The mass of a sheet of A4 paper is 5 g.

options.label: D
options.text: The heating element of an iron has a temperature of 500 K.

questions.difficultyReason: The car estimate requires a familiar mass and speed plus one kinetic-energy calculation.
questions.misconception: Overestimating everyday kinetic energy

explanation.body: A car of mass about $2000\ \mathrm{kg}$ travelling at $100\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}\approx28\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ has kinetic energy $\tfrac12mv^2=0.784\ \mathrm{MJ}$, so $100\ \mathrm{MJ}$ is unrealistic. An A4 sheet measures $210\ \mathrm{mm}\times297\ \mathrm{mm}$, giving an area of $0.062\ \mathrm{m^2}$ and a mass of about $5.0\ \mathrm{g}$ at $80\ \mathrm{g\,m^{-2}}$.

perOption.A: A laptop can draw about $50\ \mathrm W$, so this is realistic.
perOption.B: Correct. The estimate is over 100 times the example’s kinetic energy.
perOption.C: Standard $80\ \mathrm{g\,m^{-2}}$ A4 paper has a mass of about $5\ \mathrm g$ per sheet.
perOption.D: $500\ \mathrm K$ is about $227\,^\circ\mathrm C$, a plausible temperature for an iron’s heating element.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: The derived unit for which of the following quantities can be expressed in four different SI base units?
questions.stemText: The derived unit for which of the following quantities can be expressed in four different SI base units? A electromotive force B momentum C magnetic flux density D power

appearances.originalFile: grail:10416 ACJC 2023 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: Students must break several familiar derived units into base units.
questions.misconception: Counting powers instead of distinct base units.

explanation.body: Electromotive force is energy supplied per unit charge, so its unit is the joule per coulomb. Since $\mathrm{J}=\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}}$ and $\mathrm{C}=\mathrm{A\,s}$, this gives $\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-3}\,A^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Correct. It uses kilogram, metre, second and ampere.
perOption.B: Momentum has units $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$, which use three base units.
perOption.C: From $B=F/(IL)$ for a perpendicular conductor, the metre cancels and the unit is $\mathrm{kg\,s^{-2}\,A^{-1}}$.
perOption.D: Power is energy per time, with units $\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-3}}$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
The maximum theoretical power $P$ of a wind turbine is given by the equation $P=k\rho Av^n$, where $\rho$ is the density of air, $A$ is the area swept by the turbine blades, $v$ is the speed of the air and $k$ is a constant with no units.

What is the value of $n$?

A 1
B 2
C 3
D 4

stemImage.alt: Question 1: The maximum theoretical power P of a wind turbine is given by the equation P = k  A v n, where  is the density of air, A is the area swept by the turbine blad

appearances.originalFile: grail:14529 (ACJC) 2024 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: Matching the time exponents requires expressing power and speed in base units.
questions.misconception: Treating the constant as dimensional.

explanation.body: Because $k$ is dimensionless, $P$ and $\rho Av^n$ have the same base units. This gives $(\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}})(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}})=(\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}})(\mathrm{m^2})(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}})^n$, so $\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-3}}=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3+2+n}\,s^{-n}}$. Matching the powers of seconds gives $n=3$.

perOption.A: Gives a time factor of $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ for power.
perOption.B: Gives a time factor of $\mathrm{s^{-2}}$ for power.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Gives a time factor of $\mathrm{s^{-4}}$ for power.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: What is the best estimate for the time it takes light to cross the nucleus of a hydrogen atom?
questions.stemText: What is the best estimate for the time it takes light to cross the nucleus of a hydrogen atom? A $10^{-7}$ s B $10^{-15}$ s C $10^{-18}$ s D $10^{-23}$ s

appearances.originalFile: ACJC Physics/H2/2026 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1 sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Needs the order of magnitude of a nuclear diameter and the speed of light, then one division.
questions.misconception: Confusing the size of the nucleus with the size of the atom

explanation.body:
A hydrogen nucleus is about $10^{-15}\ \mathrm{m}$ across and light travels at about $10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ (order of magnitude).

Time $\approx \dfrac{10^{-15}}{10^{8}} = 10^{-23}\ \mathrm{s}$.

perOption.A: Far too long: light covers tens of metres in $10^{-7}$ s.
perOption.B: This is the size of the nucleus in metres, not the crossing time.
perOption.C: Uses the size of a whole atom (~$10^{-10}$ m) instead of the nucleus.
perOption.D: Correct. Nuclear diameter divided by the speed of light.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: The SI unit of specific heat capacity is J $\mathrm{kg}^{-1}$ $\mathrm{K}^{-1}$. What is the unit of specific heat capacity expressed in SI base units?
questions.stemText: The SI unit of specific heat capacity is J kg–1 K–1. What is the unit of specific heat capacity expressed in SI base units? A m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$ $\mathrm{K}^{-1}$ B $\mathrm{m}^{2}$ $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$ $\mathrm{K}^{-1}$ C kg m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ $\mathrm{K}^{-1}$ D kg $\mathrm{m}^{2}$ $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ $\mathrm{K}^{-1}$
questions.difficultyReason: The joule is the only derived unit that needs to be expanded.
questions.misconception: Using the dimensions of force for energy.

explanation.body: One joule is $1\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}}$. Substituting into $\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$ cancels the kilogram and leaves $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}\,K^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Uses only one factor of length in the joule.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Retains the mass unit and uses the wrong powers of length and time.
perOption.D: Retains the mass unit and uses $$\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ for the time factor.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
Quantity $X$ has a fractional uncertainty of $x$. Quantity $Y$ has a fractional uncertainty of $y$.

What is the fractional uncertainty in $\frac{3X}{Y^2}$?

A $3x+2y$
B $3x-2y$
C $x+2y$
D $x-2y$

stemImage.alt: Question 2: Quantity X has a fractional uncertainty of x. Quantity Y has a fractional uncertainty of y. 3X What is the fractional uncertainty in ? 2 Y

questions.difficultyReason: The student must handle both the exact coefficient and the squared denominator.
questions.misconception: Subtracting fractional uncertainties in division.

explanation.body: The factor of $3$ cancels when the absolute uncertainty of $3X$ is divided by $3X$, leaving $x$. Squaring $Y$ gives a fractional uncertainty of $2y$, and the fractional uncertainties add for the quotient, giving $x+2y$.

perOption.A: Incorrectly multiplies the fractional uncertainty of $X$ by 3.
perOption.B: Multiplies the fractional uncertainty of $X$ by 3 and subtracts the denominator's contribution.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Subtracts the denominator's fractional uncertainty.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: What is a reasonable estimate of the acceleration of an MRT train leaving a station in Singapore?
questions.stemText: What is a reasonable estimate of the acceleration of an MRT train leaving a station in Singapore? A 0.1 m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$ B 1 m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$ C 10 m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$ D 100 m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$

appearances.originalFile: grail:12935 2023 ASRJC H2 physics Promo P1

questions.difficultyReason: The calculation is short once a plausible speed and acceleration time are chosen.
questions.misconception: Using an unrealistic scale for everyday acceleration

explanation.body: The train starts from rest. Take $60\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}$, or about $17\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, as a representative speed reached after about $15\ \mathrm{s}$. This gives $a\approx 17/15\approx 1.1\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, so $1\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ is a reasonable estimate. This is below $g=9.81\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

perOption.A: At this acceleration the train would take about 170 s to reach the estimated speed.
perOption.B: Correct. It matches the estimated speed gain per second.
perOption.C: This would bring the train to the estimated speed in less than 2 s.
perOption.D: This is about ten times gravitational acceleration.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
The diagram shows an experiment to measure the speed of a small ball falling at constant speed through a clear liquid in a glass tube.

[A downward arrow shows the ball falling through the liquid in the vertical tube beside a rule. The upper mark is labelled $1.50\ \mathrm{s}$ and $115\ \mathrm{mm}$, and the lower mark is labelled $3.50\ \mathrm{s}$ and $385\ \mathrm{mm}$.]

There are two marks on the tube. The top mark is positioned at $115\pm1\ \mathrm{mm}$ on the adjacent rule and the lower mark at $385\pm1\ \mathrm{mm}$. The ball passes the top mark at $1.50\pm0.02\ \mathrm{s}$ and passes the lower mark at $3.50\pm0.02\ \mathrm{s}$.

The constant speed of the ball is calculated by

$\frac{385-115}{3.50-1.50}=\frac{270}{2.00}=135\ \mathrm{mm\,s^{-1}}$

Which expression calculates the fractional uncertainty in the value of this speed?

A  $\frac{2}{270}+\frac{0.04}{2.00}$
B  $\frac{2}{270}-\frac{0.04}{2.00}$
C  $\frac{1}{270}\times\frac{0.02}{2.00}$
D  $\frac{1}{270}\div\frac{0.02}{2.00}$

stemImage.alt: Question 2: The diagram shows an experiment to measure the speed of a small ball falling at constant speed through a clear liquid in a glass tube. There are two marks on th

appearances.originalFile: grail:12935 2023 ASRJC H2 physics Promo P1

questions.difficultyReason: The student must propagate uncertainties through two differences and then through a quotient.
questions.misconception: Subtracting fractional uncertainties when dividing

explanation.body: The speed is $v=(s_2-s_1)/(t_2-t_1)$. Add the absolute uncertainties within each difference, then add the fractional uncertainties for the quotient. This gives $\Delta v/v=(1+1)/270+(0.02+0.02)/2.00=2/270+0.04/2.00$.

perOption.A: Correct. Both differences and the quotient use the appropriate uncertainty rules.
perOption.B: Subtracts the fractional time uncertainty even though the fractional uncertainties add.
perOption.C: Uses single-reading uncertainties and multiplies the fractions.
perOption.D: Uses single-reading uncertainties and divides the fractions.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
When a beam of light is incident on a surface, it delivers energy to the surface. The intensity of the beam is defined as the energy delivered per unit area per unit time.

What is the unit of intensity, expressed in SI base units?
questions.stemText: When a beam of light is incident on a surface, it delivers energy to the surface. The intensity of the beam is defined as the energy delivered per unit area per unit time. What is the unit of intensity, expressed in SI base units? A kg $\mathrm{m}^{-2}$ $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ B kg $\mathrm{m}^{2}$ $\mathrm{s}^{-3}$ C kg $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$ D kg $\mathrm{s}^{-3}$

appearances.originalFile: grail:14523 ASRJC 2024 JC2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: Students must expand the joule into SI base units and cancel the area and time factors.
questions.misconception: Confusing intensity with power.

explanation.body: The intensity is $I=\frac{E}{At}$. Expressing energy in SI base units gives $\frac{(\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}})\,\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{m^2\,s}}=\mathrm{kg\,s^{-3}}$.

perOption.A: Uses $\mathrm{kg}$ as though it were the SI unit of energy.
perOption.B: Gives the unit of power by omitting division by area.
perOption.C: Omits division by time and gives the unit of energy per area.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
The diagram shows two vectors X and Y.

In which vector triangle does the vector Z show the magnitude and direction of vector X – Y?
questions.stemText: The diagram shows two vectors X and Y. Y X In which vector triangle does the vector Z show the magnitude and direction of vector X – Y? A Y X Z B Y X Z C Z X Y D Z X Y

appearances.originalFile: grail:14523 ASRJC 2024 JC2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: Students must reverse one vector and follow the head-to-tail construction.
questions.misconception: Reversing the resultant of vector subtraction.

explanation.body: Write $\mathbf Z=\mathbf X+(-\mathbf Y)$. Place the tail of $-\mathbf Y$ at the tip of $\mathbf X$, so the resultant runs from the tail of $\mathbf X$ to the tip of $-\mathbf Y$, as in A.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Reverses the required resultant and gives $\mathbf Y-\mathbf X$.
perOption.C: Adds $\mathbf X+\mathbf Y$.
perOption.D: Reverses the sum and gives $-(\mathbf X+\mathbf Y)$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: What is a reasonable estimate of the kinetic energy of a car travelling at a speed of 30 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$?
questions.stemText: What is a reasonable estimate of the kinetic energy of a car travelling at a speed of 30 m s–1? A $10^{2}$ J B $10^{4}$ J C $10^{6}$ J D $10^{8}$ J

appearances.originalFile: grail:18733 ASRJC 2025 Prelim P1 H2 Physics QN paper

questions.difficultyReason: The student needs a plausible car mass and one substitution into the kinetic-energy formula.
questions.misconception: Using an implausible car mass

explanation.body: A typical small car has a mass of about $1500\ \mathrm{kg}$. Its kinetic energy is $\frac12(1500)(30)^2\approx0.68\times10^6\ \mathrm{J}$, so $10^6\ \mathrm{J}$ is the closest estimate.

perOption.A: This energy at the stated speed would require a mass below 1 kg.
perOption.B: This energy corresponds to a mass of only about 22 kg.
perOption.C: Correct. It is the closest estimate.
perOption.D: This energy would require a mass of about 220 tonnes.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
Readings are made of the current I for different voltages V across a fixed resistor. The results are plotted on a graph to show the variation of I with V.

What is the best description of the errors in the readings?
questions.stemText: Readings are made of the current I for different voltages V across a fixed resistor. The results are plotted on a graph to show the variation of I with V. What is the best description of the errors in the readings? A random only B systematic only C both systematic and random D neither systematic nor random

appearances.originalFile: grail:18733 ASRJC 2025 Prelim P1 H2 Physics QN paper

questions.difficultyReason: The student must distinguish a consistent offset from scatter about a straight line.
questions.misconception: Confusing a nonzero intercept with random scatter

explanation.body: For a fixed resistor, $V/I=R$ is constant, so the expected $I$–$V$ line passes through the origin. The nonzero current intercept indicates a systematic error. All the points lie on the best-fit line, so there is no visible random scatter.

perOption.A: Random error would produce scatter about the line and does not explain the consistent offset.
perOption.B: Correct. The data show a systematic offset.
perOption.C: The offset is systematic, and the points show no visible scatter.
perOption.D: The nonzero intercept indicates a systematic error.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
questions.stemText: Which of the following statements is correct? A In the measurement of the diameter of a sphere, taking more readings and finding the average value of these readings will help to reduce the fractional uncertainty of the diameter. B Plotting a graph of voltage and current readings for an ohmic device and using its gradient to find resistance will help to eliminate random error. C Measuring the timing for a large number of oscillations will help to reduce the fractional uncertainty of the period. D Checking for zero error on a voltmeter before measuring a voltage will help to reduce random error.

options.label: A
options.text: In the measurement of the diameter of a sphere, taking more readings and finding the average value of these readings will help to reduce the fractional uncertainty of the diameter.

options.label: B
options.text: Plotting a graph of voltage and current readings for an ohmic device and using its gradient to find resistance will help to eliminate random error.

options.label: C
options.text: Measuring the timing for a large number of oscillations will help to reduce the fractional uncertainty of the period.

options.label: D
options.text: Checking for zero error on a voltmeter before measuring a voltage will help to reduce random error.

appearances.originalFile: ASRJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1 for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires distinguishing random/systematic errors and the effect of timing many oscillations.
questions.misconception: Confusing random and systematic errors and what each technique reduces

explanation.body: For $N$ oscillations, $T=t/N$, so $\Delta T/T=\Delta t/t$. Timing more oscillations increases $t$ while the absolute timing uncertainty $\Delta t$ stays about the same, reducing the fractional uncertainty.

perOption.A: The key assumes the diameter’s fractional uncertainty is set by the instrument, so averaging readings leaves it unchanged.
perOption.B: A best-fit gradient reduces the effect of random error without eliminating it.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: A zero error is systematic.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: Two forces $F_1$ and $F_2$ act with an angle $\theta$ between them. [Diagram: $F_1$ horizontal to the right, $F_2$ pointing up and to the right from the same point, angle $\theta$ between them.] Which combination could produce a resultant force of magnitude $1\ \mathrm{N}$? ($F_1$/N, $F_2$/N, $\theta$) A 1, 1, less than $90^\circ$ B 1, 1, more than $90^\circ$ but less than $180^\circ$ C 2, 1, less than $90^\circ$ D 2, 1, more than $90^\circ$ but less than $180^\circ$

stemImage.alt: Question 2: Two forces F1 and F2 act with an angle θ between them. F2 θ F1 Which combination could produce a resultant force of magnitude 1 N? F1 / N F2 / N θ

appearances.originalFile: ASRJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1 for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Needs reasoning about the range of resultant magnitudes for two vectors at an angle.
questions.misconception: Thinking the resultant always exceeds the larger force or forgetting angle dependence

explanation.body: Place the two $1\ \mathrm{N}$ force vectors head to tail so that they and the resultant form an equilateral triangle. The angle between the forces when drawn tail to tail is $180^\circ-60^\circ=120^\circ$, and the resultant is $1\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.A: An acute angle between the two 1 N forces gives a resultant greater than 1 N.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: The 1 N force has a positive component along the 2 N force, so the resultant exceeds 2 N.
perOption.D: A 1 N resultant from 2 N and 1 N requires the forces to be exactly opposite.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
The resistance of a resistor is measured using an ohmmeter and its reading is 47.12 Ω. The manufacturer of the ohmmeter specifies that the ohmmeter reading has an uncertainty of 10%.

How should the resistance of the resistor be recorded, along with its uncertainty?
questions.stemText: The resistance of a resistor is measured using an ohmmeter and its reading is 47.12 Ω. The manufacturer of the ohmmeter specifies that the ohmmeter reading has an uncertainty of 10%. How should the resistance of the resistor be recorded, along with its uncertainty? A (47 ± 5) Ω B (47.1 ± 0.1) Ω C (47.1 ± 4.7) Ω D (47.12 ± 5) Ω

appearances.originalFile: grail:16130 2022 H2 CJC Physics Promo Paper 1 QP

questions.difficultyReason: Converts a percentage uncertainty and rounds the reading to match.
questions.misconception: Reporting excess precision

explanation.body: The absolute uncertainty is $47.12\times10\%=4.71\ \Omega$, which rounds to $5\ \Omega$ to one significant figure. Round the reading to the same place to obtain $(47\pm5)\ \Omega$.

perOption.A: Correct. Both values are reported to the nearest ohm.
perOption.B: Uses an uncertainty much smaller than the stated 10%.
perOption.C: Keeps two significant figures in the uncertainty under the school's one-significant-figure convention.
perOption.D: Keeps hundredths of an ohm when the uncertainty is rounded to whole ohms.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A man of mass $75.2\ \mathrm{kg}$ uses a set of weighing scales to measure his mass three times. He obtains the following readings.

mass / kg
reading 1  80.2
reading 2  80.1
reading 2  80.2

Which statement describes the precision and accuracy of the weighing scales?

A  not precise to $\pm 0.1\ \mathrm{kg}$ and accurate to $\pm 0.1\ \mathrm{kg}$
B  not precise to $\pm 0.1\ \mathrm{kg}$ and not accurate to $\pm 0.1\ \mathrm{kg}$
C  precise to $\pm 0.1\ \mathrm{kg}$ and accurate to $\pm 0.1\ \mathrm{kg}$
D  precise to $\pm 0.1\ \mathrm{kg}$ and not accurate to $\pm 0.1\ \mathrm{kg}$

stemImage.alt: Question 1: A man of mass 75.2 kg uses a set of weighing scales to measure his mass three times. He obtains the following readings. mass / kg reading 1 80.2 reading 2 80.1

questions.difficultyReason: Students compare the spread and the offset from a known mass.
questions.misconception: Equating repeatability with accuracy

explanation.body: The readings are about $5\ \mathrm{kg}$ from the man’s true mass, so the scales are inaccurate to $\pm 0.1\ \mathrm{kg}$. The repeated readings differ by only $0.1\ \mathrm{kg}$, so they are precise to the stated tolerance.

perOption.A: The readings cluster tightly and lie well outside the accuracy tolerance.
perOption.B: The readings are close enough to satisfy the precision tolerance.
perOption.C: The readings are about 5 kg above the true mass.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A car is travelling west with a speed of $15\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

[Top view of a car with a leftward arrow labelled $15\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. A compass shows north up, east right, south down and west left.]

A drone moving south flies over the car with a speed of $20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

At this instant, which arrow represents the velocity of the drone relative to the car?

A [Steep arrow pointing down and right.]
B [Steep arrow pointing up and left.]
C [Shallower arrow pointing down and right.]
D [Shallower arrow pointing up and left.]

stemImage.alt: Question 1: A car is travelling west with a speed of 15 m s-1. car 15 m s-1 A drone moving south flies over the car with a speed of 20 m s-1. At this instant, which arrow r

questions.difficultyReason: The student must subtract the car’s velocity and compare the direction of the resultant with the arrows.
questions.misconception: Adding velocities for relative motion

explanation.body: The drone’s velocity relative to the car is $\vec v_{\mathrm{drone}}-\vec v_{\mathrm{car}}$. Add $20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ south to $15\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ east to obtain a direction $\tan^{-1}(15/20)=36.9^\circ$ east of south, closest to arrow A.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Points northwest, opposite to the required southeast direction.
perOption.C: Points southeast but is farther from the required angle of $36.9^\circ$ east of south.
perOption.D: Points northwest, opposite to the required southeast direction.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
Which length is equal to $1\ \mathrm{dm}$?
A $1\times10^0\ \mathrm{mm}$
B $1\times10^1\ \mathrm{mm}$
C $1\times10^0\ \mathrm{cm}$
D $1\times10^1\ \mathrm{cm}$

stemImage.alt: Question 1: Which length is equal to 1 dm?

questions.difficultyReason: Uses a single SI prefix conversion.
questions.misconception: Confusing deci-, centi- and milli-

explanation.body: One decimetre is $1\times10^{-1}\ \mathrm{m}$. This equals $1\times10^2\ \mathrm{mm}$ or $1\times10^1\ \mathrm{cm}$.

perOption.A: One millimetre is a hundredth of a decimetre.
perOption.B: Ten millimetres are a tenth of a decimetre.
perOption.C: One centimetre is a tenth of a decimetre.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: Measurements $a$, $b$ and $c$ are taken to determine the quantity $x$ which is given by $x = \dfrac{ab^2}{c}$. The total uncertainty of $x$ is calculated to be 12%. Which individual percentage uncertainties of $a$, $b$ and $c$ when combined give this total of 12%? [Table a/%, b/%, c/%] A: 4, 2, 4. B: 2, 8, 2. C: 3, 2, 2. D: 6, 2, 4.

stemImage.alt: Question 1: Measurements a, b and c are taken to determine the quantity x which is given by 2 ab x .  c The total uncertainty of x is calculated to be 12 %. Which individu

questions.difficultyReason: Single application of the rule for combining percentage uncertainties with a power.
questions.misconception: Forgetting to multiply the uncertainty of a squared quantity by its power

explanation.body: For $x=ab^2/c$, the fractional uncertainty is $\Delta x/x=\Delta a/a+2\Delta b/b+\Delta c/c$. In percentage terms, option A gives $(4+2(2)+4)\%=12\%$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Doubling the contribution from $b$ gives $20\%$.
perOption.C: Doubling the contribution from $b$ gives $9\%$.
perOption.D: Doubling the contribution from $b$ gives $14\%$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
On a football field, a player P is moving north with a speed of 3.0 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ and a player Q is moving east with a speed of 1.0 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$.

Which arrow represents the velocity of the player P relative to the player Q?
questions.stemText: On a football field, a player P is moving north with a speed of 3.0 m s-1 and a player Q is moving east with a speed of 1.0 m s-1. Q P 3.0 m s-1 -1 1.0 m s Which arrow represents the velocity of the player P relative to the player Q? A  B  C  D
questions.difficultyReason: Needs vector subtraction for relative velocity, a common slip in direction.
questions.misconception: Adding velocities instead of subtracting, or finding Q relative to P

explanation.body: The velocity of P relative to Q is $\mathbf v_P-\mathbf v_Q=\mathbf v_P+(-\mathbf v_Q)$. Add the $1.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ westward vector to the tip of the $3.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ northward vector to obtain the steep northwest arrow.

perOption.A: Points southeast and understates the north–south component.
perOption.B: Points northwest but understates the northward component relative to the westward component.
perOption.C: Reverses the relative velocity and shows Q moving relative to P.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.stemText:
The frequency $f$ of vibration of a mass $m$ supported by a spring with spring constant $k$ is given by the equation

$f=Cm^pk^q$

where $C$ is a constant with no units.

What are the values of $p$ and $q$?

[Columns are $p$ and $q$.]
A $-\frac12$, $-\frac12$
B $-\frac12$, $\frac12$

questions.misconception: Adding displacement magnitudes as scalars.

questions.difficultyReason: The student must combine opposite pairs and then add the remaining forces as vectors.
questions.misconception: Adding nonparallel forces as scalars

explanation.body: Each opposite pair leaves $300\,\mathrm N$, respectively along $OD$, $OE$ and $OF$. The components of the $OD$ and $OF$ forces perpendicular to $OE$ cancel, and their components along $OE$ add to $2(300)\cos60^\circ=300\,\mathrm N$. Including the third force gives $600\,\mathrm N$ along $OE$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Reverses the resultant direction.
perOption.C: Adds the three $300\,\mathrm N$ forces as scalars.
perOption.D: Adds nonparallel forces as scalars and reverses the resultant direction.

The measurements and the associated uncertainties of a spherical object are given below

diameter: $(1.85\pm0.01)\ \mathrm{cm}$
mass: $(12.6\pm0.1)\ \mathrm{g}$

What is the uncertainty of density as determined from the above measurements?

A $(3.80\pm0.02)\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$
B $(3.80\pm0.05)\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$
C $(3.80\pm0.06)\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$
D $(3.8\pm0.1)\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$

appearances.originalFile: grail:12812 EJC 2021 J1 H2 Promo P1 QP

questions.difficultyReason: The student must propagate two fractional uncertainties through a cubic dependence and round the result.
questions.misconception: Omitting the factor of three in the diameter uncertainty

explanation.body: Using the volume of a sphere, $\rho=\dfrac{6m}{\pi d^3}=\dfrac{6(12.6)}{\pi(1.85)^3}=3.8006\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$. The fractional uncertainty is $\dfrac{\Delta\rho}{\rho}=\dfrac{\Delta m}{m}+3\dfrac{\Delta d}{d}$. Substituting gives $\Delta\rho=3.8006(0.1/12.6+3\times0.01/1.85)\approx0.092\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$. perOption.B: Adding the mass and diameter fractional uncertainties without tripling the diameter term gives about this value.
perOption.C: Tripling the diameter term but omitting the mass uncertainty gives about this value.

As part of the 1945 Manhattan project, the United States Army tested the first-of-its-kind nuclear weapon in New Mexico.

The explosion resulted in a radiant, hemispherical blast wave of radius $R$ which could be modelled using $R=s\left(\frac{Et^2}{\rho}\right)^{0.2}$

where $E$ = energy released due to explosion,
$t$ = time elapsed after detonation,
$\rho$ = density of air.

What is the SI unit of the quantity $s$?

A (dimensionless)
B $\mathrm{m^{0.2}}$
C $\mathrm{J^{0.2}\,m^{-0.2}\,s^{0.4}\,kg^{-0.2}}$
D $\mathrm{J^{-1}\,m^2\,s^{-2}\,kg}$

stemImage.alt: Question 2: As part of the 1945 Manhattan project, the United States Army tested the first-of-its-kind nuclear weapon in New Mexico. The explosion resulted in a radiant, he

questions.difficultyReason: Requires simplifying a derived unit raised to a fractional power.
questions.misconception: Incorrect cancellation of SI base units

explanation.body: Rearrange to $s=R(Et^2/\rho)^{-0.2}$. The units of $Et^2/\rho$ are $(\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}})(\mathrm{s^2})/(\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}})=\mathrm{m^5}$, so the units of $s$ reduce to $\mathrm{m}(\mathrm{m^5})^{-0.2}=1$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Leaves a residual power of metres even though $(\mathrm{m^5})^{0.2}=\mathrm{m}$.
perOption.C: Reduces to $\mathrm{m^{0.2}}$, leaving a residual length dimension.
perOption.D: Also dimensionless because a joule is a kilogram metre squared per second squared.

questions.stemText:
A car is travelling at $80\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}$ due east and a lorry is travelling at $50\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}$ with a bearing of $300^\circ$. What is the relative velocity of the lorry with respect to the car?

A. $126\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}$, bearing $281.5^\circ$
B. $126\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}$, bearing $101.4^\circ$
C. $126\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}$, bearing $78.5^\circ$
D. $44\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}$, bearing $5.4^\circ$

stemImage.alt: Question 2: A car is travelling at 80 km h−1 due east and a lorry is travelling at 50 km h−1 with a bearing of 300°. What is the relative velocity of the lorry with respect

appearances.originalFile: grail:12817 EJC 2022 J1 H2 PROMO QP PAPER 1

questions.difficultyReason: Subtracting two velocity vectors requires constructing a triangle and converting its angle to a bearing.
questions.misconception: Reversing the order of relative velocity subtraction.

explanation.body:
The lorry’s velocity relative to the car is $\mathbf v_{LC}=\mathbf v_L+(-\mathbf v_C)$. The cosine rule on the velocity triangle gives $v_{LC}^2=50^2+80^2-2(50)(80)\cos150^\circ$, so $v_{LC}=126\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}$.

The sine rule gives $80/\sin\theta=126/\sin150^\circ$, so $\theta=18.5^\circ$. The bearing is $360^\circ-18.5^\circ-60^\circ=281.5^\circ$.

perOption.A: Correct. The resultant points north of west.
perOption.B: Reverses the relative velocity, giving a direction approximately opposite to the required one.
perOption.C: Places the resultant east of north by measuring the acute angle on the wrong side of north.
perOption.D: Uses a small resultant consistent with adding the original velocities instead of subtracting the car’s velocity.

Which of the following statements is correct?
A A reading is inaccurate when it is not precise.
B Checking for zero error on a micrometer before making a measurement will help to reduce random error.
C Measuring the time taken for a larger number of oscillations will help to reduce the fractional uncertainty of the period of each oscillation.
D To determine the diameter of a sphere, taking more measurements and finding the average value of these measurements will reduce the fractional uncertainty of the diameter.

stemImage.alt: Question 2: Which of the following statements is correct? A A reading is inaccurate when it is not precise. B Checking for zero error on a micrometer before making a measur

appearances.originalFile: grail:12822 EJC 2023 J1 H2 Promo P1 QP

questions.difficultyReason: Students distinguish random error, systematic error and fractional uncertainty when comparing measurement procedures.
questions.misconception: Confusing longer timing intervals with averaging at fixed instrument uncertainty

explanation.body: Timing 5 or 20 oscillations gives $t_5=5T$ or $t_{20}=20T$, so $\Delta T/T=\Delta t_5/t_5$ or $\Delta t_{20}/t_{20}$, respectively. The stopwatch timing uncertainty is the same in both cases, $\Delta t_5=\Delta t_{20}=\Delta t$. Since $t_{20}>t_5$, timing more oscillations gives a smaller fractional uncertainty in $T$.

perOption.A: Confuses accuracy, which concerns closeness to the true value, with precision, which concerns repeatability.
perOption.B: Checking for zero error addresses a systematic offset.
perOption.C: Correct. The same absolute timing uncertainty is divided by a longer interval.
perOption.D: Under the key’s instrument-uncertainty model, propagating four equal bounds through the average still gives $(4\Delta d)/4=\Delta d$.

Given that $\mu=\dfrac{vL\rho}{R}$

where $v$ is the velocity of the fluid, $L$ the characteristic length and $\rho$ is the density of the fluid.

What is the unit of $R$, expressed in SI units?

A $\mathrm{kg\,N^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$
B $\mathrm{kg\,N^{-1}\,m^{-3}\,s^{-2}}$
C $\mathrm{m^{-2}\,s^{-2}}$

questions.misconception: Failing to expand the newton into SI base units

$a=\dfrac{b-c}{d^2}$

The numerical values of $b$, $c$ and $d$ in their SI units are:

$b=25\pm3$, $c=4\pm1$ and $d=100\pm1$.

A 12%

questions.stemText: What is the number of heartbeats of a person at rest in one hour, to the nearest order of magnitude? A $10^{1}$ B $10^{2}$ C $10^{3}$ D $10^{5}$
questions.difficultyReason: A single rate estimate and time conversion are sufficient.
questions.misconception: Confusing a per-minute rate with an hourly count.

explanation.body: Estimate the resting rate as one heartbeat per second. This gives about $3600$ beats in an hour, so $10^3$ is the closest listed power of ten.

perOption.A: Ten beats is on the scale of seconds at the estimated resting rate.
perOption.B: This is closer to a count over a minute than over an hour.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: This would require about 28 beats per second for an hour.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: Which experimental technique reduces the systematic error of the quantity being investigated?
questions.stemText: Which experimental technique reduces the systematic error of the quantity being investigated? A measuring the diameter of a wire repeatedly and calculating the average B measuring several internodal distances on a standing wave to find the mean internodal distance C adjusting an analogue ammeter to remove its zero error before measuring a current D timing a large number of oscillations to find a period

options.label: A
options.text: measuring the diameter of a wire repeatedly and calculating the average

options.label: B
options.text: measuring several internodal distances on a standing wave to find the mean internodal distance

options.label: C
options.text: adjusting an analogue ammeter to remove its zero error before measuring a current

options.label: D
options.text: timing a large number of oscillations to find a period

questions.difficultyReason: Students must recognising a zero error as a fixed offset identifies the technique directly.
questions.misconception: Expecting repeated measurements to remove a fixed offset.

explanation.body: A nonzero ammeter reading at zero current is a systematic offset. Adjusting the ammeter to read zero before taking measurements removes that offset.

perOption.A: Averaging repeated readings reduces random scatter but leaves a persistent offset.
perOption.B: Averaging spacings reduces the effect of random node-location errors without correcting a systematic bias.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Timing many oscillations reduces the fractional timing uncertainty without removing an instrument bias.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: What is the order-of-magnitude of the mass of twelve one-dollar (\$1) Singapore coins?
questions.stemText: What is the order-of-magnitude of the mass of twelve one-dollar ($1) Singapore coins? A $10^{0}$ g B $10^{1}$ g C $10^{2}$ g D $10^{3}$ g
questions.difficultyReason: Uses a familiar mass estimate and scales it to twelve coins.
questions.misconception: Estimating the mass of one coin instead of twelve

explanation.body: One coin has a mass of order $10^1\ \mathrm{g}$. Twelve coins have a total mass of order $10^2\ \mathrm{g}$.

perOption.A: This is approximately the mass of one paper clip.
perOption.B: This is approximately the mass of one coin.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: A kilogram is an unreasonably large estimate for twelve coins.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A student takes measurements to calculate the density of a liquid in a beaker.

The height of the liquid is $0.20\ \mathrm{m}\pm2\%$.

The internal diameter of the beaker is $0.05\ \mathrm{m}\pm3\%$.

The mass of the liquid is $0.36\ \mathrm{kg}\pm10\%$.

What is the percentage uncertainty in the calculated density of the liquid?

A. $2\%$
B. $5\%$
C. $15\%$
D. $18\%$

stemImage.alt: Question 2: A student takes measurements to calculate the density of a liquid in a beaker. The height of the liquid is 0.20 m ± 2%. The internal diameter of the beaker is 0

questions.difficultyReason: Requires expressing density in terms of the measurements and doubling the diameter contribution.
questions.misconception: Counting the diameter uncertainty only once

explanation.body: The volume is $\pi(d/2)^2h$, so the density is $\rho=4m/(\pi h d^2)$. Adding the percentage uncertainties, with the diameter contribution doubled, gives $10\%+2(3\%)+2\%=18\%$.

perOption.A: This counts only the height uncertainty.
perOption.B: This leaves out the mass uncertainty and counts the diameter uncertainty only once.
perOption.C: This counts the diameter uncertainty only once despite the squared diameter.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: A ball bearing is drop from rest and it took time $t$ to fall for a distance $h$ where $h = \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$. The reading for $t$ is $t = (0.4000 \pm 0.0008)\ \mathrm{s}$. What is the maximum percentage uncertainty in $h$ such that the gravitational acceleration $g$ can be determined with a maximum uncertainty of $\pm 2\%$? A 1.6% B 1.8% C 2.2% D 2.4%

stemImage.alt: Question 1: A ball bearing is drop from rest and it took time t to fall for a distance h where 1 2 g t2 h = The reading for t is t = (0.4000  0.0008) s What is the maximum

questions.difficultyReason: Rearranging the fractional-uncertainty sum with the power of 2 on t.
questions.misconception: Forgetting to double the percentage uncertainty in t, or adding instead of subtracting

explanation.body: Rearranging gives $g=2h/t^2$. The maximum fractional uncertainties add as $\frac{\Delta g}{g}=\frac{\Delta h}{h}+2\frac{\Delta t}{t}$. The maximum percentage uncertainty in $h$ is therefore $2.0\%-2(0.0008/0.4000)\times100\%=1.6\%$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Subtracts the time uncertainty only once, forgetting the squared time in the denominator.
perOption.C: Adds the time uncertainty once instead of subtracting it twice.
perOption.D: Adds the doubled percentage uncertainty in time to the 2% budget.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
In FIFA World Cup 2026, the Adidas’ Triondas football was the official football model.

What is the approximate volume of the football?
questions.stemText: In FIFA World Cup 2026, the Adidas’ Triondas football was the official football model. What is the approximate volume of the football? A $10^{-6}$ $\mathrm{m}^{3}$ B $10^{-3}$ $\mathrm{m}^{3}$ C $10^{-1}$ $\mathrm{m}^{3}$ D $10^{3}$ $\mathrm{m}^{3}$
questions.difficultyReason: Single order-of-magnitude estimate from everyday knowledge.
questions.misconception: Poor sense of scale when converting cm to m³

explanation.body: Estimate the football’s diameter as $20\ \mathrm{cm}=0.20\ \mathrm{m}$, giving a radius of $0.10\ \mathrm{m}$. The volume scales as $r^3$, and $\frac{4}{3}\pi(0.10)^3\approx 4\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^3}$, closest to $10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^3}$.

perOption.A: Implies a sphere only about a centimetre across.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses the surface area $4\pi r^2$, which is measured in $\mathrm{m^2}$.
perOption.D: Implies a sphere over ten metres across.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: Which of the following is considered as a random error?
questions.stemText: Which of the following is considered as a random error? A Error as a result of using g = 10 m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$, instead of g = 9.81 m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$. B Error in measuring the time duration of a 100 m sprint using a stopwatch. C Error due to a stopwatch running too fast. D Zero error of a measuring instrument.

options.label: A
options.text: Error as a result of using g = 10 m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$, instead of g = 9.81 m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$.

options.label: B
options.text: Error in measuring the time duration of a 100 m sprint using a stopwatch.

options.label: C
options.text: Error due to a stopwatch running too fast.

options.label: D
options.text: Zero error of a measuring instrument.

questions.difficultyReason: Identifying the variable reaction delay distinguishes the one random error from three consistent biases.
questions.misconception: Confusing random variation with consistent bias

explanation.body: Using an approximate value of $g$, a fast stopwatch or an instrument with zero error biases results consistently, so these are systematic errors. When timing a sprint manually, variations in reaction time can make the measured duration higher or lower, giving a random error.

perOption.A: The same approximation for $g$ consistently biases results.
perOption.B: Correct. Reaction times vary between measurements.
perOption.C: A fast stopwatch consistently overstates elapsed times.
perOption.D: Zero error shifts readings consistently in one direction.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
Which of the following is not a reasonable estimate?

A. Sound of frequency in the order of $10^9\ \mathrm{Hz}$ is audible to human beings.
B. Light of wavelength in the order of $10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}$ is visible to human beings.
C. The volume of an average-sized orange is in the order of $10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^3}$.
D. The speed of beta particles emitted from a nucleus is in the order of $10^7\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

stemImage.alt: Question 1: Which of the following is not a reasonable estimate?

questions.difficultyReason: The student must judge orders of magnitude across several physical contexts.
questions.misconception: Overestimating the upper limit of human hearing.

explanation.body: Visible wavelengths of order $10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}$ and beta-particle speeds of order $10^7\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ are reasonable estimates. Using $V=\frac43\pi r^3$ with an orange radius of about $5\ \mathrm{cm}$ gives a volume of order $10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^3}$. A frequency of $10^9\ \mathrm{Hz}$ is far above the range of human hearing.

perOption.A: Correct. A gigahertz is far above the audible range.
perOption.B: Visible wavelengths are typically several times $10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}$.
perOption.C: The volume of a sphere of radius about $5\ \mathrm{cm}$ is of order $10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^3}$.
perOption.D: A speed of order $10^7\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ is plausible for a beta particle.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
The kinetic energy $E_{\mathrm{k}}$ of a rotating solid sphere is given by the following expression

$E_{\mathrm{k}}=\frac{2\pi^2 I}{T^2}$

where $I$ is the moment of inertia and $T$ is the period of rotation of the solid sphere.

What is the unit for the moment of inertia $I$, expressed in SI base units?

A. $\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-1}}$
B. $\mathrm{kg\,m^2}$
C. $\mathrm{J\,s^2}$
D. $\mathrm{N\,m\,s^2}$

stemImage.alt: Question 2: The kinetic energy EK of a rotating solid sphere is given by the following expression  2 2 I = E k 2 T where I is the moment of inertia and T is the period of

questions.difficultyReason: The student must rearrange the formula and express kinetic energy in base units.
questions.misconception: Leaving derived units in an SI base-unit answer.

explanation.body: Rearrange $E_{\mathrm{k}}=2\pi^2I/T^2$ to $I=E_{\mathrm{k}}T^2/(2\pi^2)$. Kinetic energy has the units of $mv^2$, so the unit of $I$ is $(\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}})(\mathrm{s^2})=\mathrm{kg\,m^2}$.

perOption.A: This leaves an extra inverse second after multiplying by the squared time unit.
perOption.B: Correct. The time units cancel completely.
perOption.C: The joule is a derived unit and needs to be expanded into base units.
perOption.D: The newton is a derived unit and needs to be expanded into base units.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A ruler is supported horizontally by two pivots as shown.

[The ruler bows down between two pivots, one at each end. Its vertical displacement $y$ at the centre is measured from a dashed horizontal line between the ends.]

The vertical displacement $y$ at the centre of the ruler can be used to measure the mass loaded on it and is given by the equation

$y=\frac{kML^3}{wt^3}$

where $k$ is a constant, $L$ is the distance between the pivots, $M$ is the mass loaded onto the ruler, $t$ is the thickness of the ruler and $w$ is the width of the ruler.

When a particular $M$ is loaded onto the ruler, the following results are obtained:

$y=(0.25\pm0.01)\ \mathrm{mm}$
$L=(80.0\pm0.2)\ \mathrm{cm}$
$t=(6.0\pm0.1)\ \mathrm{mm}$
$w=(23.0\pm0.5)\ \mathrm{mm}$

Which measurement contributes the most to the uncertainty of $M$?

A. $y$
B. $L$
C. $t$
D. $w$

stemImage.alt: Question 3: A ruler is supported horizontally by two pivots as shown. y The vertical displacement y at the centre of the ruler can be used to measure the mass loaded on it

questions.difficultyReason: The student must rearrange for mass and compare four fractional uncertainties weighted by their powers.
questions.misconception: Comparing fractional uncertainties without weighting by the exponents.

explanation.body: Rearrange to $M=ywt^3/(kL^3)$, so $\Delta M/M=\Delta y/y+\Delta w/w+3\Delta t/t+3\Delta L/L$. The contributions from $y$ and $w$ are $0.01/0.25=0.040$ and $0.5/23.0=0.022$. The contributions from $t$ and $L$ are $3(0.1/6.0)=0.050$ and $3(0.2/80.0)=0.0075$. The thickness $t$ contributes the most.

perOption.A: The unweighted contribution of 0.040 is smaller than the thickness contribution.
perOption.B: Even after tripling the fractional uncertainty, the contribution is only 0.0075.
perOption.C: Correct. The cubed thickness contributes 0.050.
perOption.D: The width contributes only 0.022.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
The speed of an aeroplane in still air is $200\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}$. The wind pushes it from the west at a speed of $85.0\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}$.

In which direction must the pilot steer in order to fly due north?

A. $23.0^\circ$ east of north
B. $23.0^\circ$ west of north
C. $25.2^\circ$ east of north
D. $25.2^\circ$ west of north

stemImage.alt: Question 4: The speed of an aeroplane in still air is 200 km h−1. The wind pushes it from the west at a speed of 85.0 km h−1. In which direction must the pilot steer in ord

questions.difficultyReason: The student must construct a velocity triangle with an eastward wind and a due-north resultant.
questions.misconception: Treating the still-air speed as the northward component.

explanation.body: The plane’s velocity relative to Earth is $\vec v_{\mathrm{PE}}=\vec v_{\mathrm{PW}}+\vec v_{\mathrm{WE}}$, where the terms on the right are the plane’s velocity relative to the wind and the wind’s velocity relative to Earth. The velocity triangle requires the plane’s westward component to cancel the eastward wind, so $\sin\theta=85/200$ and the pilot steers $25.2^\circ$ west of north.

perOption.A: This uses the tangent with 200 as the northward component and steers in the direction of the wind.
perOption.B: This uses the tangent with 200 as the northward component, although it is the hypotenuse.
perOption.C: An eastward heading component adds to the eastward wind.
perOption.D: Correct. The westward component cancels the wind.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A quantity x is measured many times and the number N of measurements giving a value of x is plotted against x. The true value of the quantity is $x_{o}$.

Which graph best represents precise measurements with poor accuracy?
questions.stemText: A quantity x is measured many times and the number N of measurements giving a value of x is plotted against x. The true value of the quantity is xo. Which graph best represents precise measurements with poor accuracy? A  B  C  D
questions.difficultyReason: Requires identifying the spread and centre of a measurement distribution.
questions.misconception: Confusing precision with accuracy

explanation.body: Precision corresponds to a small spread in repeated measurements. Poor accuracy means their centre is displaced from the true value $x_0$. Graph B shows a narrow peak away from $x_0$.

perOption.A: The measurements are precise and centred on $x_0$, so they are also accurate.
perOption.B: Correct. The narrow peak is displaced from the true value.
perOption.C: The peak is displaced, but its broad spread indicates poor precision.
perOption.D: The broad peak indicates poor precision, and its centre is at $x_0$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
Errors in measurement may be either systematic or random.

Which of the following involves random error?
questions.stemText: Errors in measurement may be either systematic or random. Which of the following involves random error? A Not allowing for zero error on an analog voltmeter B Not subtracting background count rate when determining the count rate from a radioactive source C Stopping a stopwatch at the end of a race D Using the value of g as 10 N $\mathrm{kg}^{-1}$ when calculating weight from mass

options.label: A
options.text: Not allowing for zero error on an analog voltmeter

options.label: B
options.text: Not subtracting background count rate when determining the count rate from a radioactive source

options.label: C
options.text: Stopping a stopwatch at the end of a race

options.label: D
options.text: Using the value of g as 10 N $\mathrm{kg}^{-1}$ when calculating weight from mass

questions.difficultyReason: Requires distinguishing variable timing error from a consistent measurement bias.
questions.misconception: Treating background count fluctuations and omission of the background correction as the same error

explanation.body: The reaction time when stopping a stopwatch varies from trial to trial, introducing random scatter in the measured times. The other examples introduce consistent biases through an offset, an uncorrected background contribution or an approximate constant.

perOption.A: A voltmeter zero error gives readings a consistent offset.
perOption.B: Leaving the mean background count rate in the result systematically overestimates the source count rate.
perOption.C: Correct. The stopwatch operator’s reaction time varies between trials.
perOption.D: Using $10\ \mathrm{N\,kg^{-1}}$ where $g=9.81\ \mathrm{N\,kg^{-1}}$ systematically overestimates weight.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
1 The base units of the SI system include those of

mass, kg;    length, m;    time, s;    electric current, A.

Which base units would be needed to express the SI unit of potential difference (the volt)?

A m and A only.
B s and A only.
C m, s and A only.
D kg, m, s and A.

stemImage.alt: Question 1: The base units of the SI system include those of mass, kg; length, m; time, s; electric current, A. Which base units would be needed to express the SI unit of p

questions.difficultyReason: Expand work and charge into SI base units to find the units of voltage.
questions.misconception: Dropping mass when expanding the unit of force

explanation.body: Potential difference is work per unit charge, so $V=W/Q=Fs/(It)=mas/(It)$, where $s$ is displacement. This gives $\mathrm{V}=\frac{\mathrm{kg}\cdot\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\cdot\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{A}\cdot\mathrm{s}}=\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-3}\,A^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Omits the mass and time units in the derived unit.
perOption.B: Accounts for the base units of charge but omits mass and length from work.
perOption.C: Omits the mass unit in the newton.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A single sheet of aluminium foil is folded twice to produce a stack of four sheets. The total thickness of the stack of sheets is measured to be $(0.80\pm0.02)\ \mathrm{mm}$. This measurement is made using a digital calliper with zero error of $(-0.20\pm0.02)\ \mathrm{mm}$.

What is the percentage uncertainty in the calculated thickness of a single sheet?

A $1.0\%$
B $2.0\%$
C $4.0\%$
D $6.7\%$

stemImage.alt: Question 1: A single sheet of aluminium foil is folded twice to produce a stack of four sheets. The total thickness of the stack of sheets is measured to be (0.80  0.02) m

questions.difficultyReason: Correct the zero error and propagate both uncertainties.
questions.misconception: Subtracting uncertainties when subtracting readings.

explanation.body: Subtract the negative zero error and add the absolute uncertainties to get $4t=(1.00\pm0.04)\ \mathrm{mm}$. Dividing by four gives $t=(0.25\pm0.01)\ \mathrm{mm}$. The percentage uncertainty is $(0.01/0.25)\times100\%=4.0\%$.

perOption.A: Divides the uncertainty by four while retaining the stack thickness as the denominator.
perOption.B: Includes only one of the two absolute uncertainties.
perOption.C: Correct. Both the thickness and its uncertainty scale by one quarter.
perOption.D: Subtracts the magnitude of the zero error and uses a thickness of 0.60 mm.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A voltmeter connected across a resistor in a circuit gives readings which have high precision but low accuracy.

Which of the following best describes the likely error in readings taken with this voltmeter?

| Option | random error | systematic error |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | high | high |
| B | high | low |
| C | low | high |
| D | low | low |

stemImage.alt: Question 2: A voltmeter connected across a resistor in a circuit gives readings which have high precision but low accuracy. Which of the following best describes the likely

questions.difficultyReason: Match precision to scatter and accuracy to closeness to the true value.
questions.misconception: Confusing precision with accuracy.

explanation.body: High precision means repeated readings are tightly clustered, so random error is low. Low accuracy despite the small scatter indicates a large systematic error that shifts the readings away from the true value.

perOption.A: High random error would spread the readings out and reduce precision.
perOption.B: High random error contradicts the stated high precision.
perOption.C: Correct. The readings have little scatter and a large systematic offset.
perOption.D: Low systematic and random errors would give readings close to the true value.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: The kinetic energy E of an object rotating about its centre of mass is $E = \frac{1}{2}k\omega^2$, where $\omega$ is the angular speed of rotation and k is a constant. What is the unit for k? A $\mathrm{kg\,m^2}$ B $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$ C $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$ D $\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-4}}$

stemImage.alt: Question 1: The kinetic energy E of an object rotating about its centre of mass is calculated using 1 = k 2 E 2 where  is the angular speed of rotation, and k is a consta

questions.difficultyReason: Single rearrangement of SI base units.
questions.misconception: Forgetting that angular speed has unit $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ or misexpressing the joule

explanation.body: Rearrange the expression to $k=2E/\omega^2$. Since radians are dimensionless, the unit of $k$ is $(\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}})(\mathrm{s^{-1}})^{-2}=\mathrm{kg\,m^2}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Gives the units of linear momentum instead of dividing the energy units by angular speed squared.
perOption.C: Gives the units of force and loses a power of length from the energy units.
perOption.D: Multiplies the energy units by angular speed squared instead of dividing.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: The following measurements were taken of a uniform metal disc: mass $m = (265.2 \pm 0.5)$ g, diameter $D = (10.3 \pm 0.1)$ cm, thickness $t = (1.36 \pm 0.02)$ cm, electrical resistance $R = (20 \pm 1)\ \Omega$. The density $\rho$ of the disc is determined using the above measurements. Which measurement contributes the most to the uncertainty of $\rho$? A m B D C t D R

stemImage.alt: Question 2: The following measurements were taken of a uniform metal disc. mass m = (265.2  0.5) g diameter D = (10.3  0.1) cm thickness t = (1.36  0.02) cm electrical r

questions.difficultyReason: Compare fractional uncertainties with the power of D, and ignore the irrelevant R.
questions.misconception: Comparing absolute instead of fractional uncertainties, or including irrelevant data

explanation.body: The density is $\rho=m/(\pi D^2t/4)$. The percentage uncertainty contributions are $0.19\%$ from mass, $2(0.97\%)=1.94\%$ from diameter, and $1.5\%$ from thickness. The diameter contributes the most.

perOption.A: Mass contributes only $0.19\%$.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Thickness appears to contribute the most if the diameter’s percentage uncertainty is counted only once.
perOption.D: Resistance does not enter the density calculation.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: Which of the following contains only SI base units?
questions.stemText: Which of the following contains only SI base units? A kilogram, metre, mole, ampere B metre, mole, ampere, mass C kelvin, kilogram, coulomb, second D ampere, kelvin, gram, mole

appearances.originalFile: grail:16186 2017 RI H2 Physics Prelims P1 QP

questions.difficultyReason: The question requires recognising the SI base units and distinguishing them from a quantity and a derived unit.
questions.misconception: Treating gram as the SI base unit for mass

explanation.body: SI base units include the kilogram for mass, metre for length, mole for amount of substance and ampere for electric current. All four entries in A are base units.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Mass is a physical quantity measured in kilograms.
perOption.C: The coulomb is derived from the ampere and second.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
Which of the following estimates is not reasonable?

A The average density of a car is about $300\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$.
B The mass of one sheet of paper in this booklet is about $5\ \mathrm{g}$.
C The useful power delivered by a crane in lifting a $1000\ \mathrm{kg}$ concrete block is about $10^4\ \mathrm{W}$.
D A typical classroom in RI contains about $3000\ \mathrm{mol}$ of air molecules at room temperature.

stemImage.alt: Question 2: Which of the following estimates is not reasonable?

appearances.originalFile: grail:16186 2017 RI H2 Physics Prelims P1 QP

questions.difficultyReason: The student must assess several order-of-magnitude estimates, including an ideal-gas estimate with a plausible classroom volume.
questions.misconception: Underestimating the moles of air in a classroom

explanation.body: A classroom about $10\ \mathrm{m}\times10\ \mathrm{m}\times3\ \mathrm{m}$ has volume $300\ \mathrm{m^3}$. At room temperature (about $300\ \mathrm{K}$) and atmospheric pressure (about $10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}$), use $n=pV/(RT)$. The key’s substitution, $(10^5\times300)/(8.31\times288)$, gives approximately $1.3\times10^4\ \mathrm{mol}$, several times the stated $3000\ \mathrm{mol}$.

perOption.A: A typical $1500\ \mathrm{kg}$ car occupies roughly $5\ \mathrm{m^3}$, giving a density of about $300\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$.
perOption.B: An A4 sheet measuring $210\ \mathrm{mm}\times297\ \mathrm{mm}$ at $80\ \mathrm{g\,m^{-2}}$ has a mass of about $5\ \mathrm{g}$.
perOption.C: At a lifting speed of about $1\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, the useful power is $mgv\approx10^3\times10\times1=10^4\ \mathrm{W}$.
perOption.D: Correct. The estimated amount of air is several times larger.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
The density of a liquid is calculated by measuring its mass and its volume. The measurements taken are as shown.
Mass of beaker $=(20\pm1)\ \mathrm{g}$
Mass of beaker and liquid $=(70\pm1)\ \mathrm{g}$
Volume of liquid $=(10.0\pm0.6)\ \mathrm{cm^3}$

The density of the liquid calculated is $5.0\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$. What is the uncertainty in this value of density?
A. $0.1\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$
B. $0.4\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$
C. $0.5\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$
D. $2.6\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$

stemImage.alt: Question 1: The density of a liquid is calculated by measuring its mass and its volume. The measurements taken are as shown. ( ) mass of beaker 20 1 g = ± ( ) mass of beake

appearances.originalFile: grail:16192 2018 RI H2 Physics Prelims P1 QP

questions.difficultyReason: The calculation switches from absolute uncertainty for subtraction to fractional uncertainty for division.
questions.misconception: Using the same uncertainty rule for subtraction and division

explanation.body: The liquid has mass $70-20=50\ \mathrm{g}$ with absolute uncertainty $1+1=2\ \mathrm{g}$. For $\rho=m_{\mathrm{liq}}/V_{\mathrm{liq}}$, the fractional uncertainty is $\Delta\rho/\rho=2/50+0.6/10.0$. Multiplying by $5.0\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$ gives $\Delta\rho=0.5\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$ to one significant figure.

perOption.A: Reports the fractional uncertainty $0.10$ as though it were the absolute uncertainty.
perOption.B: Counting only one of the two mass-reading uncertainties gives this value.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Adds the raw mass and volume uncertainties despite their different units.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
The Planck length is hypothesised to be the smallest possible length at which current physical laws still apply.

It is related to the following fundamental constants: reduced Planck constant $\hbar=h/2\pi$, the gravitational constant $G$ and the speed of light $c$.

Which expression could be correct for the Planck length?

A $\frac{\hbar G}{c^3}$
B $\left(\frac{\hbar G}{c^3}\right)^{1/2}$
C $\left(\frac{\hbar G}{c^3}\right)^{1/3}$
D $\left(\frac{\hbar G}{c^2}\right)^{1/3}$

stemImage.alt: Question 1: The Planck length is hypothesised to be the smallest possible length at which current physical laws still apply.   , the It is related to the following fundam

appearances.originalFile: grail:16202 2020 RI Prelims H2 Phy Paper 1 QP

questions.difficultyReason: The student must reduce three derived units to base units and apply the expression’s outer power.
questions.misconception: Ignoring the dimensions before taking the root

explanation.body: The units of $(\hbar G/c^3)^{1/2}$ are $\left[(\mathrm{J\,s})(\mathrm{N\,m^2\,kg^{-2}})/(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}})^3\right]^{1/2}$. In base units this is $\left[(\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-1}})(\mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}\,s^{-2}})/(\mathrm{m^3\,s^{-3}})\right]^{1/2}=(\mathrm{m^2})^{1/2}=\mathrm m$.

perOption.A: Without the square root, the units are $\mathrm{m^2}$.
perOption.B: Correct. The square root gives metres.
perOption.C: The cube root gives units of $\mathrm{m^{2/3}}$.
perOption.D: Using only the square of the speed of light in the denominator leaves a time dimension.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A physical quantity $P$ is described by the relation $P^2=a^{1/2}b^2c^{-3}d^4$.

If the percentage errors in the measurements of $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ are 4%, 2%, 6% and 5% respectively, what is the percentage error in $P$?

A 4%
B 8%
C 22%
D 44%

stemImage.alt: Question 2:   2 1 2 2 3 4 P a b c d A physical quantity P is described by the relation . If the percentage errors in the measurements of a, b, c and d are 4%, 2%, 6% and

appearances.originalFile: grail:16202 2020 RI Prelims H2 Phy Paper 1 QP

questions.difficultyReason: The student must take the square root before adding percentage uncertainties weighted by the resulting exponents.
questions.misconception: Subtracting the uncertainty of a factor with a negative exponent

explanation.body: Taking the square root gives $P=(a^{1/2}b^2c^{-3}d^4)^{1/2}=a^{1/4}bc^{-3/2}d^2$. Add the fractional uncertainties weighted by the magnitudes of the powers: $\Delta P/P=\Delta a/(4a)+\Delta b/b+3\Delta c/(2c)+2\Delta d/d$. The percentage error is $\tfrac14(4\%)+2\%+\tfrac32(6\%)+2(5\%)=1\%+2\%+9\%+10\%=22\%$.

perOption.A: Subtracts the contribution from $c$ because its exponent is negative.
perOption.B: Subtracts the contribution from $c$ and uses the powers for $P^2$.
perOption.C: Correct. The four weighted percentage errors add to 22%.
perOption.D: Uses the percentage error in $P^2$ as the percentage error in $P$.

questions.stemText:
In an experiment to determine the density of a sphere, the following measurements are made.
mass = $(80\pm2)\ \mathrm g$
diameter = $(4.0\pm0.1)\ \mathrm{cm}$

How should the value of density of the sphere be expressed?

A. $(2.4\pm0.1)\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$
B. $(2.4\pm0.2)\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$
C. $(2.4\pm0.4)\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$
D. $(2\pm2)\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$

stemImage.alt: Question 1: In an experiment to determine the density of a sphere, the following measurements are made. mass =    g 80 2 diameter =    cm 4.0 0.1 How should the value

appearances.originalFile: grail:16209 2021 RI Prelims H2 Phy Paper 1 QP

questions.difficultyReason: It requires propagating the cubed diameter’s uncertainty and matching decimal places.
questions.misconception: Omitting the factor of three in the diameter uncertainty.

explanation.body: The density is $\rho=m/(\tfrac43\pi r^3)=80/[\tfrac43\pi(2.0)^3]=2.3873\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$. The fractional uncertainty is $\Delta\rho/\rho=\Delta m/m+3\Delta d/d=2/80+3(0.1/4.0)=0.10$. The absolute uncertainty is $0.24\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$, which rounds to $0.2\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$ to one significant figure, so $\rho=(2.4\pm0.2)\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$.

perOption.A: Treats diameter as a first-power quantity and understates the uncertainty.
perOption.B: Correct. The absolute uncertainty rounds to 0.2.
perOption.C: Overstates the absolute uncertainty implied by the 10% fractional uncertainty.
perOption.D: Gives an uncertainty as large as the rounded density, far above the calculated 10%.

How should the student record the speed of sound, considering the uncertainty?

A $330\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
B $335.6\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
C $336\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
D $340\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$

questions.misconception: Rounding the measured value independently of its uncertainty

explanation.body: The absolute uncertainty is $\Delta v=(4.5/100)(335.61)=15.1\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, which rounds to $20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ to one significant figure. Round the measured speed to the tens place as well to obtain $(340\pm20)\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.B: Keeps the tenths place, which is finer than the rounded uncertainty supports.

questions.stemText:
The Stefan-Boltzmann law for the rate of thermal energy emitted per unit surface area of a body is given by

$\dfrac{P}{A}=e\sigma T^4$,

where $P$ is the rate of thermal energy emitted, $A$ is the surface area, $T$ is the thermodynamic temperature and $e$, a dimensionless constant, is the emissivity of the body and $\sigma$ is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant.

Which is the S.I. base unit for $\sigma$?

A $\mathrm{kg\,s^{-3}\,K^{-4}}$
B $\mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}\,K^{4}}$
C $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,K^{-4}}$
D $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,{}^\circ C^{-4}}$

stemImage.alt: Question 2: The Stefan-Boltzmann law for the rate of thermal energy emitted per unit surface area of a body is given by P   4 e T , A where P is the rate of thermal energ

appearances.originalFile: grail:16215 2022 RI Prelims H2 Phy Paper 1 QP

questions.difficultyReason: The student isolates the constant and resolves power into base units using work and force.
questions.misconception: Leaving watts in an expression for SI base units

explanation.body: Rearrange to $\sigma=P/(AeT^4)$, where $e$ is dimensionless. Power is work per unit time, and work has the units of force times distance, so the units are those of $mad/(tAeT^4)$. This reduces to $(\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}})(\mathrm m)/(\mathrm{s\,m^2\,K^4})=\mathrm{kg\,s^{-3}\,K^{-4}}$.

perOption.A: Correct. The metres cancel when power is expressed in base units.
perOption.B: Uses the wrong time exponent and puts the temperature factor in the numerator.
perOption.C: Gives equivalent derived units but leaves the watt unexpanded.
perOption.D: Uses both an unexpanded watt and degrees Celsius instead of kelvin.

A vector $F$ can be resolved into two perpendicular components $F_1$ and $F_2$. The angle between $F$ and $F_2$ is $\theta$.

[From a common origin, $F$ points up, $F_1$ points up-left and $F_2$ points up-right. The marked angle $\theta$ is between $F$ and $F_2$.]

How do the magnitudes of $F_1$ and $F_2$ change as $\theta$ is increased from $0^\circ$ to $90^\circ$?

[Each option gives the change in $F_1$ followed by the change in $F_2$.]
A increase, increase
B increase, decrease
C decrease, increase
D decrease, decrease

stemImage.alt: Question 1: A vector F can be resolved into two perpendicular components F1 and F2. The angle between F and F2 is . F F2  F1 How do the magnitudes of F1 and F2 change as

appearances.originalFile: grail:10474 2023 RI  H2 Physics Prelims P1 Questions

questions.difficultyReason: The two limiting angles show how the components of a fixed vector vary.
questions.misconception: Swapping the components relative to the marked angle

explanation.body: When $\theta=0^\circ$, $F_2=F$ is largest and $F_1=0$ is smallest. When $\theta=90^\circ$, $F_2=0$ is smallest and $F_1=F$ is largest. Thus $F_1$ increases and $F_2$ decreases.

perOption.A: Predicts that both components increase even though $F_2$ falls to zero.
perOption.B: Correct. $F_1$ increases and $F_2$ decreases.
perOption.C: Swaps the component along the marked angle with the perpendicular component.

questions.stemText:
The speed $v$ of a liquid leaving a tube depends on the difference in pressure $\Delta P$ between the ends of the tube and the density $\rho$ of the liquid according to the equation

$v=k\left(\frac{\Delta P}{\rho}\right)^n$

where $k$ is a unitless constant.

What is the value of $n$?
A $\frac12$
B $1$
C $\frac32$
D $2$

stemImage.alt: Question 1:  The speed v of a liquid leaving a tube depends on the difference in pressure P between the ends of the tube and the density  of the liquid according to the e

appearances.originalFile: grail:14582 2024 RI Prelim H2 Phy Paper 1

questions.difficultyReason: The student must convert pressure and density to base units and compare exponents.
questions.misconception: Leaving the units of squared speed unchanged

explanation.body: Pressure has units $\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$ and density has units $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$. Thus $(\Delta P/\rho)^n$ has units $\mathrm{m^{2n}\,s^{-2n}}$. Matching these to $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ gives $2n=1$, so $n=\frac12$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Leaves the units as $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$.

What is the percentage uncertainty in the difference of the two diameters?
A $0.29\%$
B $0.58\%$

perOption.B: Correct. The narrow distribution is offset from the true value.

A student determines the resistivity $\rho$ of a wire using

$\rho = \dfrac{\pi d^2 V}{4IL}$

where $d$ is the diameter of the wire, $L$ is its length, $V$ is the potential difference across the wire and $I$ is the current through it.

The percentage uncertainty in the measurements of $d$, $L$, $V$ and $I$ are 3%, 2%, 1% and 0.5% respectively.

What is the percentage uncertainty in $\rho$?

A 4.5%   B 6.5%   C 7.5%   D 9.5%

stemImage.alt: Question 2: A student determines the resistivity  of a wire using  2 d V = I 4 L where d is the diameter of the wire, L is its length, V is the potential difference acro

appearances.originalFile: RI/H2/2026 RI H2Phy Prelims P1 Questions.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: A routine application of the rule for combining percentage uncertainties.
questions.misconception: Subtracting uncertainties for quantities in the denominator

explanation.body:
For $\rho = \dfrac{\pi d^2 V}{4IL}$, the percentage uncertainties add, with $d$ counted twice because it is squared:

$\%\rho = 2(\%d) + \%V + \%I + \%L = 2(3\%) + 1\% + 0.5\% + 2\% = 9.5\%$

perOption.A: Subtracts the uncertainties of the denominator quantities $I$ and $L$ instead of adding them.
perOption.B: Forgets to double the uncertainty in $d$ even though $d$ is squared.
perOption.C: Leaves out the uncertainty in $L$.
perOption.D: Correct. Percentage uncertainties add, with $d$'s counted twice.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A period $T$ of a type of pendulum is given by

$T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{I}{K}}$.

If $I$ has a unit of $\mathrm{kg\,m^2}$, which of the following can be a unit of $K$?

A. $\mathrm{N\,m}$
B. $\mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$
C. $\mathrm{kg\,m^2}$
D. $\mathrm{s^{-2}}$

stemImage.alt: Question 1: A period T of a type of pendulum is given by I =  T 2 K If I has a unit of kg m2, which of the following can be a unit of K?

questions.difficultyReason: It requires accounting for the square root and recognizing a named derived unit.

explanation.body: Squaring the period equation and keeping just units gives $\mathrm{s^2}=(\mathrm{kg\,m^2})/[K]$, where $[K]$ is the unit of $K$. Thus $[K]=\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}}=(\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}})\mathrm{m}=\mathrm{N\,m}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Dividing newtons by metres cancels the length dimension needed in the result.
perOption.C: Keeps the units of $I$ and omits the inverse-square time factor.
perOption.D: Keeps the inverse-square time factor but drops the units of $I$.

Which arrow best shows the change in velocity of the object?

questions.misconception: Reversing initial and final vectors

explanation.body: The change in velocity is final minus initial, so $\Delta\mathbf v=\mathbf y-\mathbf x$. With the tails together, the arrow from the tip of $\mathbf x$ to the tip of $\mathbf y$ points down and right.

What is the mass of the object, including its absolute uncertainty?

A. $(0.17\pm0.01)\ \mathrm{kg}$
B. $(0.17\pm0.03)\ \mathrm{kg}$
C. $(0.45\pm0.01)\ \mathrm{kg}$
D. $(0.45\pm0.02)\ \mathrm{kg}$

questions.difficultyReason: Requires deriving the mass and propagating uncertainties through a subtraction and a division.
questions.misconception: Treating relative uncertainty as absolute uncertainty

explanation.body: Taking downward as positive gives $mg-U=ma$, so $m=U/(g-a)=2.40/(9.81-4.50)=0.451977\ \mathrm{kg}$. The fractional uncertainty is $\Delta m/m=0.06/2.40+0.05/(9.81-4.50)=0.034416$. Multiplying by the mass gives $\Delta m=0.015555\ \mathrm{kg}$, which rounds to $0.02\ \mathrm{kg}$, so the result is $(0.45\pm0.02)\ \mathrm{kg}$.

perOption.A: Uses $g+a$ in the denominator, as if the object accelerated upward.
perOption.B: Uses $g+a$ and overstates the absolute uncertainty for that mass.
perOption.C: Undercounts the uncertainty, for example by including only the upthrust contribution.

A micrometer is used to measure the diameters of two cylinders.

The difference in the diameters is calculated. What is the percentage uncertainty in this difference?

B 0.58

questions.difficultyReason: Compare means and ranges from a small data table and apply accuracy versus precision.

explanation.body:
Average of $h$ (in $10^{-34}$ J s): A 6.63, B 6.63, C 6.65, D 6.62.

A, B and D are accurate (close to the accepted 6.63).

Range of variation: A 0.04, B 0.02, C 0.07, D 0.02. B and D are precise.

questions.stemText: The relation between the velocity $v$ of waves in the sea with its wavelength $\lambda$, the surface tension $\gamma$ and density $\rho$ of sea water is given by $v = k\sqrt{\dfrac{\gamma}{\lambda\rho}}$, where $k$ = constant of proportionality. If $\gamma$ = (4.30 $\pm$ 0.05) N m$^{-1}$, $\rho$ = (1450 $\pm$ 20) kg m$^{-3}$ and the percentage uncertainty in $\lambda$ is 5%, what is the percentage uncertainty in the velocity of the waves? A 2%; B 3%; C 4%; D 8%.

stemImage.alt: Question 3: The relation between the velocity v of waves in the sea with its wavelength, the surface tension and density of sea water is given by:  v = k  where k = c

questions.difficultyReason: Needs the rule for uncertainty with a power and a quotient, with three contributing terms.
questions.misconception: Forgetting to multiply the summed fractional uncertainty by the power 1/2.

explanation.body:
$v = k\sqrt{\dfrac{\gamma}{\lambda\rho}}$, so the power of $1/2$ applies to the sum of the fractional uncertainties.

$\dfrac{\Delta v}{v} \times 100\% = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{0.05}{4.30} + \dfrac{20}{1450} + 0.05\right) \times 100\% = 3.8\% \approx 4\%$.

perOption.A: Too small: underestimates the sum of the terms.
perOption.B: Too small: underestimates the sum of the terms.
perOption.C: Correct. 3.8%, which rounds to 4%.
perOption.D: Does not apply the power $1/2$ (adds the fractional uncertainties without halving: 7.5%).

questions.stemText: Which one of the following estimates is unrealistic? A The potential energy of a man at the top of Bukit Timah Hill is 100 kJ. B The volume of air in a classroom is 150 $\mathrm{m}^{3}$. C The mass of an apple is 100 g D The average temperature of fire is 300 K.

options.label: A
options.text: The potential energy of a man at the top of Bukit Timah Hill is 100 kJ.

options.label: B
options.text: The volume of air in a classroom is 150 $\mathrm{m}^{3}$.

options.label: C
options.text: The mass of an apple is 100 g

options.label: D
options.text: The average temperature of fire is 300 K.

questions.difficultyReason: Simple order-of-magnitude estimates; converting 300 K to 27 °C makes D obvious.

explanation.body:
A: Bukit Timah Hill is about 160 m high, so $E_p = mgh = (60)(9.81)(160) = 94\ \mathrm{kJ}$, close to 100 kJ.

B: A classroom is about $7 \times 8 \times 3 = 147\ \mathrm{m^3}$, close to 150 m³.

C: 100 g for an apple is reasonable.

D: 300 K is only 27 °C, which is unrealistic for the temperature of a fire.

perOption.A: Realistic: $mgh = (60)(9.81)(160) \approx 94$ kJ.
perOption.B: Realistic: a $7 \times 8 \times 3$ m room holds about 147 m³ of air.
perOption.C: Realistic: an apple has a mass of about 100 g.
perOption.D: Correct. 300 K is about room temperature (27 °C), far too low for fire.

What is the value, with its absolute uncertainty, of the surface area of the cylinder? A (280 ± 10) $\mathrm{cm}^{2}$ B (282.7 ± 0.2) $\mathrm{cm}^{2}$ C (420 ± 30) $\mathrm{cm}^{2}$ D (424.1 ± 0.3) $\mathrm{cm}^{2}$

appearances.originalFile: grail:14610 YIJC 2024 JC2 PRELIM H2 Phy P1 QP

questions.difficultyReason: Standard propagation of fractional uncertainty with correct rounding.
questions.misconception: Adding absolute uncertainties for a product

explanation.body:
Surface area of the open cylinder: $A = 2\pi rL = 282.7\ \mathrm{cm^2}$.

$\dfrac{\Delta A}{A} = \dfrac{\Delta r}{r} + \dfrac{\Delta L}{L}$, so $\Delta A = \left(\dfrac{0.1}{3.0} + \dfrac{0.1}{15.0}\right)(282.7) = 10\ \mathrm{cm^2}$ (to 1 s.f.).

Therefore $A = (280 \pm 10)\ \mathrm{cm^2}$.

perOption.A: Correct. Fractional uncertainties add to 4%, and the value is rounded to match the uncertainty.
perOption.B: Adds the absolute uncertainties instead of the fractional ones, and quotes too many significant figures.
perOption.C: Calculates the volume $\pi r^2 L$, not the curved surface area.
perOption.D: Calculates the volume $\pi r^2 L$ with a wrongly propagated uncertainty and too many significant figures.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
Which estimate is realistic?

A The frequency of a radio wave is $3\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{Hz}$.
B The kinetic energy of a cyclist along East Coast Park is $1\times10^3\ \mathrm{J}$.
C The mass of an atom is $1\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{kg}$.
D The momentum of a car on an expressway is $2\times10^6\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$.

stemImage.alt: Question 1: Which estimate is realistic?

appearances.originalFile: YIJC/2026 JC2 H2 Prelim Paper 1 QP (Revised).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Use typical everyday and atomic scales to evaluate four different estimates.
questions.misconception: Confusing everyday or atomic orders of magnitude.

explanation.body: Taking the cyclist’s mass as $80\ \mathrm{kg}$ and speed as $5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ gives $E_k=\tfrac12(80)(5)^2=1000\ \mathrm J$, so B is realistic. From $v=f\lambda$, a $10\ \mathrm m$ radio wave has frequency $3\times10^7\ \mathrm{Hz}$. An atom with mass number 1 to 200 has a mass of order $10^{-27}$ to $10^{-25}\ \mathrm{kg}$, and a $1000\ \mathrm{kg}$ car at $12\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ has momentum $1.2\times10^4\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: The frequency is far too low, with a $10\ \mathrm m$ radio wavelength giving $3\times10^7\ \mathrm{Hz}$.
perOption.B: Correct. A cyclist can have about $1\ \mathrm{kJ}$ of kinetic energy.
perOption.C: Atomic masses are typically of order $10^{-27}$ to $10^{-25}\ \mathrm{kg}$.
perOption.D: The estimate is far too high, as $1000\ \mathrm{kg}$ at $12\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ gives $1.2\times10^4\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$.
